analysis.one_liner: Requires insurance to cover sexual assault forensic exams with no patient cost sharing.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had a Democratic sponsor and Republican cosponsors, was referred to three House committees and a subcommittee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require group health plans and health insurers to pay the full cost of a medical forensic exam for a sexual assault patient — the exam for injuries, the interview, and evidence collection — with no deductible, copay, or coinsurance. It would apply to out-of-network exam providers too, so a survivor could not be billed extra for seeing a nurse examiner outside her plan's network. The rules would take effect for plan years starting in 2025. In states where a state program already covers the full out-of-pocket cost, the mandate would not apply, and insurers would have to tell patients how to seek state reimbursement when a claim is denied.
analysis.who_benefits: Survivors of sexual assault who have private health insurance. A forensic exam after an assault can involve thousands of dollars in charges; the bill would guarantee they pay nothing out of pocket, including when the exam is done by a sexual assault nurse examiner who is not in their plan's network. Providers of these exams would also benefit, since insurers rather than patients or state programs would pay the bill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sexually assaulted patients with private insurance

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover forensic medical exams — the trauma exam, the determination of penetration or force, the patient interview, and evidence collection — with no cost sharing [S2][S3].
Applies the ban on surprise out-of-network billing to these exams, so a survivor treated by an examiner outside her plan's network could not be billed the balance [S3].

Applies regardless of whether the examiner has a contract with the plan, and adds a safe harbor so a high-deductible health plan can cover the exam before the deductible without losing that status [S3].
Requires plans that deny a claim or impose cost sharing in exempt states to tell the patient how to seek reimbursement from the state and, with her consent, notify the state agency [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group health plans, who would absorb the cost of exams that patients currently pay for out of pocket or that state victim-compensation programs reimburse. Premiums could rise slightly to cover it. The cost is small because forensic exams are a narrow category of care.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to people with private insurance; uninsured survivors would still depend on state compensation programs or pay nothing through other routes, and the bill does nothing for them [S3].
In states where the state program already covers the full out-of-pocket cost, the mandate does not apply, so the bill's protection varies by where a survivor lives [S3].
The rules would not take effect until plan years beginning January 1, 2025, delaying relief for more than two years after introduction [S3].
Insurers and self-insured employers would bear new mandated costs, a small but real addition to premiums for a benefit used by a narrow group [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to survivors is real and targeted: it removes out-of-pocket bills and network traps at one of the worst moments in a person's life. The cost to insurers and employers is narrow — a single type of exam — and the main design weakness is that coverage depends on having private insurance in the first place, which excludes the uninsured survivors most likely to be financially vulnerable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in its three assigned committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means — and its health subcommittee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on September 19, 2022, joined by Reps. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin and Carol Miller of West Virginia, with four cosponsors in total — three Democrats and one Republican [S1][S3][S4].

The House referred it to three committees with jurisdiction, and the next day it went to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee; no further action was recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, nothing changed: health insurers and employer plans avoided the new no-cost-sharing mandate, and survivors with private insurance continued to face exam bills or to rely on state victim-compensation programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employer health plans, unchanged status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — three Democrats and one Republican cosponsored — and no one is recorded as opposing it; the bill died from committee inaction, not from a party fight.

industries.note: The bill would force plans to cover forensic exams in full, including out-of-network examiners, removing the cost sharing they can currently shift to patients. The dollar amount is small, and the industry's interest in avoiding the mandate runs against survivors' interest in free exams.
Self-insured employer plans governed by ERISA would carry the same no-cost-sharing mandate, adding a modest benefit cost.

industries.industry: Sexual assault forensic examiners and hospitals providing them
industries.note: Insurers, not survivors or state programs, would pay for exams — including out-of-network ones treated like emergency care — so providers would face fewer unpaid or disputed bills.
In states that do not already pay full out-of-pocket exam costs, insurers would take over; in states that do, the state programs remain the payer and the mandate does not apply.
